newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Lazarenko resigns, Kuchma accepts.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Lazarenko resigns, Kuchma accepts.

text.p: Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma ended speculation about the fate of his controversial prime minister, Pavlo Lazarenko, by saying he had accepted his resignation on Wednesday.
"The resignation is accepted, and there will be a decree later today," Kuchma told reporters.
Kuchma, speaking at a joint news conference with visiting Czech President Vaclav Havel, said a new candidate for prime minister would be named after consultations with parliament.

The decision, which followed months of speculation about Lazarenko's links to the energy sector and a campaign by Ukrainian and Western officials to dismiss him, means Kuchma will have to re-appoint the entire cabinet.
He will also need approval from 226 deputies in the 450-seat parliament for any candidate, and Kuchma said negotiations would be held with the chamber before he proposed anyone for the post.
Kuchma issued a decree on June 19 appointing Lazarenko's deputy, Vasyl Durdynets, acting prime minister, a move which was seen as heralding Lazarenko's departure from power.

Potential replacements include Anatoly Kinakh, head of the Ukrainian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, and Serhiy Tyhypko, deputy minister in charge of reforms, who has an image as a youthful reformer able to boost Ukraine's standing abroad.
The head of Kuchma's administration, Yevhen Kushnaryov, has also been lobbying for Oleh Dyomin, governor of the eastern Kharkiv region, sources close to the administration say.
Local media have also said Olexander Tkachenko, a prominent leftist and first deputy speaker in the conservative-dominated parliament, could be in the running.
Durdynets, the acting prime minister, is a former police general seen as loyal to Kuchma but lacking charisma and the support he would need in parliament to approve his appointment.

Lazarenko took over as prime minister in May 1996 from Yevhen Marchuk, who was accused of mishandling the economy and self-promotion. In turn, he was blamed in part for slow privatisation and failing to stamp out government corruption.
Lazarenko entered hospital on June 19 but some aides said the wording of the original decree, which said he was being replaced because of illness, was just a ploy.

The chief doctor at the elite government hospital at Feofaniya outside Kiev said at first that it was very likely that Lazarenko, 44, would have an operation for severe varicose veins in the legs which could cause a heart attack or stroke.

But the doctor said last week that Lazarenko, a solid, dark, bespectacled figure, might still have an operation and could not comment on his state, saying simply: "His condition is the condition of someone who is undergoing medical tests."
Lazarenko's top aide said he was suffering from exhaustion and Kuchma's spokesman said he "unfortunately" had no idea what kind of illness Lazarenko had.
Western media have said that Lazarenko was behind Ukraine's biggest gas trader, the United Energy Systems of Ukraine, and alleged that he received $200 million in revenues.
He was the initiator and backer of a scheme introduced in 1995 which involved private companies distributing gas on the Ukrainian market. He denies any personal gain.
Kuchma has slammed Lazarenko's government for failing to push through reforms and this year's budget, which did not receive parliament's approval until June 27.

Ukraine desperately needs to implement reforms to qualify for a multi-billion-dollar payment from the International Monetary Fund, which says it may give Kiev an interim stand-by deal instead until it meets the rest of a list of 41 conditions.
